title: The mustard seed
hook: Kisa Gotami seeks medicine for her dead child from a house where no one has died (Therigatha commentary)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abba Joseph lifted fingers like ten lamps and said: become all flame. Your line was all flame. What did you do all the way through? Day seventy-five.

Today's story is a tender one, so let's go slowly. Most of us know what happens right after a loss. The world keeps moving, and it feels wrong that it does. People say things that don't help. You may find yourself looking for the one thing, the one call or the one answer, that would undo it. Around two and a half thousand years ago, in northern India, a young mother named Kisa Gotami went looking for exactly that. The Buddhist texts remember her walk. Today's story is the mustard seed.
screen: `AFTER A LOSS.` → `LOOKING FOR THE ONE THING.` → `KISA GOTAMI'S WALK.`

segments.voice: Her name, Kisa Gotami, means something like Gotami the thin one. The story is told in the old Buddhist commentaries, on the poems of the early nuns and on the Dhammapada. She married, and she had a little boy. When he was just old enough to walk, he fell sick and died. And she couldn't accept it. She picked him up and carried him on her hip from house to house in the city, asking everyone for medicine for her son. People turned away, or thought she had lost her mind. Finally someone sent her to the Buddha. And he didn't argue with her. He didn't explain. He said: yes, I can help. Bring me a mustard seed, from a house where no one has ever died. Mustard seed was in every kitchen. It was the easiest thing in the world to ask for. So she went. At the first house, they said: of course, take some. And then: but we lost our father last year. At the next house, a daughter. At the next, a husband, a grandmother, a baby. Every door would give her the seed. No door could give her the seed she needed. Somewhere along that street, the story says, she understood. Death wasn't something that had singled her out. It was in every house. She laid her son down, gently, and came back to the Buddha, and later she became a nun, remembered as one of the wise women of early Buddhism. Look at how the Buddha taught her. Not with a sermon. With a walk, and a houseful of neighbors who knew her grief from the inside. Her sorrow wasn't taken away. She just wasn't alone in it anymore.
screen: `A MOTHER CARRIES HER SON.` · `BRING ONE MUSTARD SEED.` · `EVERY HOUSE HAS LOST SOMEONE.` · `SHE WASN'T ALONE IN IT.` · then, large: `NO HOUSE WITHOUT IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember someone you've lost, gently. Settle, and breathe. If there's someone, let them come to mind: a face, a voice, a small ordinary moment. You don't have to do anything with it. If tears come, let them. Then, for a moment, think of the other houses on your street, in your town, in the world, where someone is remembering too, right now. Your grief is yours, and it's also in good company. If no one comes to mind, hold someone who's grieving. The bell holds the time.
The mustard seed. The seed every house could give, and no house could give from a home untouched by death. Today's word.
Your line: no house without it. Today, if you pass someone who's grieving, remember that your house knows it too. A small, kind word is enough. Day seventy-five.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often tell the story of Kisa Gotami at funerals and in teaching on impermanence, and she is honored as one of the enlightened nuns whose verses are kept in the Therigatha.

fork.setup: you're the Buddha. a young mother brings her dead son and begs you for medicine. what do you do?
options: explain gently that nothing can be done
ask her for a mustard seed from a house where no one has died
tell her to stop grieving and let go
fork.reveal: he asks for a mustard seed from a house untouched by death. every house offers the seed; none is untouched. on that walk, she understands.

original.note: Pali, written here in Devanagari: kisa means thin or lean; Gotami is her family name.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha played a trick on a grieving mother.
what it means: he let her find, door by door, that death is in every house, and she isn't alone.
what a scholar hears: the full tale is in the commentaries on the Therigatha and Dhammapada, not the verses themselves.

notes: Story paraphrased. Confirm the Therigatha verse numbers for Kisa Gotami (213–223) and the Dhammapada commentary verse (often given as 114; some cite 287).
Kisa = thin, lean (Pali kisa): confirm. Devanagari spelling किसा गोतमी: confirm.

Tone: a grief lesson. The practice offers an alternative for those without a loss in mind. A Buddhist scholar should check the phrase 'remembered as one of the wise women of early Buddhism' (she is traditionally named foremost among nuns in wearing coarse robes).
